title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1): Semantics and Content
summary: Defines what HTTP/1.1 messages mean: request methods, header fields, response status codes, payload handling, and content negotiation. It is one of the documents that replaced RFC 2616. It was later replaced by RFC 9110.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP/1.1 is the version of the web's request and response protocol that was in use for decades. This RFC says what each part of a request and a response means: that GET fetches a copy of a thing, that PUT replaces it, that a 404 means the server could not find it. It also explains how a server and a browser agree on which version of a page, language or compression to send.

subtitle: What each HTTP request method, status code and header field actually means.

tldr.problem: HTTP/1.1 had grown a large and inconsistent body of rules about what each method, header field and status code meant, spread across RFC 2616 and its many updates.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the semantics of HTTP/1.1 messages: the request methods and their safe, idempotent and cacheable properties, the request and response header fields, the status code classes, the payload and the mechanisms for content negotiation.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7231 is a Proposed Standard from June 2014 and has been obsoleted by RFC 9110, which restates the semantics of HTTP messages. The unit metadata also lists RFC 2817 as updated by it.

sections.title: What HTTP/1.1 Messages Mean
sections.content:
HTTP is a stateless, application-level protocol for distributed, collaborative, hypertext information systems. This RFC defines the semantics of HTTP/1.1 messages as expressed by request methods, request header fields, response status codes and response header fields, together with the payload of messages and the mechanisms for content negotiation.

The split matters. The message syntax, parsing and routing are defined in RFC 7230; this document is about meaning. The RFC states that a message is semantically invalid if it is disallowed by this specification or if the framing is invalid under RFC 7230, and that the robustness principle applies: a recipient of an invalid message should either reject it or continue with the parts it understands.

One design goal runs through the document: separating the identification of a resource from the meaning of the request. That is achieved by putting the request semantics in the method and in a few request-modifying header fields, so that the same URI can be fetched, replaced or removed depending on the method used. If the meaning implied by the URI itself conflicts with the meaning of the method, the method wins.
sections.plainLanguage: This document does not describe how to write down a request; it describes what the pieces mean once written. The method carries most of the meaning, and where the URI suggests something different, the method decides.

sections.title: Resources and Representations
sections.content:
The target of a request is a resource, and HTTP does not limit what a resource can be. It merely defines an interface for interacting with one. Each resource is identified by a Uniform Resource Identifier.

Because a resource could be anything, HTTP needs an abstraction for the current or desired state of that thing. That abstraction is a representation: information intended to reflect a past, current or desired state of a resource, in a format that can be communicated over the protocol, made up of representation metadata and a potentially unbounded stream of representation data. An origin server may have several representations of one resource, and an algorithm selects the one most applicable to a given request, usually by content negotiation. The selected representation supplies the data and metadata used to evaluate conditional requests and to build the payload of a 200 response to GET.

The representation metadata travels in header fields. Four of them describe the representation: Content-Type, Content-Encoding, Content-Language and Content-Location. They are what let a client interpret the payload. When the payload is a media type, the type and subtype are case-insensitive, and a parameter value that matches the token production may be written either bare or inside a quoted string, the two forms being equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: A resource is the thing on the other end. A representation is one particular form of it, in a particular format and language, with a set of headers describing how to read it. A server can hold several forms and pick the one that suits the request.

sections.title: Safe, Idempotent and Cacheable Methods
sections.content:
A method is safe when its semantics are essentially read-only: the client neither requests nor expects any state change on the server. The definition does not stop an implementation from doing something harmful as a side effect, because what matters is that the client did not ask for it and cannot be held responsible. Logging every request is an example that is still considered safe. Of the methods this RFC defines, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are safe.

The point of the distinction is that automated retrieval and cache prefetching can then work without fear of causing harm, and a user agent can warn a person before an unsafe action. The RFC adds a practical rule: if a resource is built so that a query parameter selects an action, such as a delete link expressed as a query parameter, then the owner must disable that action when it is reached with a safe method, because link maintenance and search indexers issue GET requests for every URI they find.

A method is idempotent when the intended effect of several identical requests is the same as the effect of one. PUT, DELETE and the safe methods are idempotent. The property is about what was requested: a server may still log each request separately. Idempotent methods matter because a request can be repeated automatically when a connection fails before the response is read, and the client then knows the repeat will have the same effect even if the first attempt succeeded.

Methods can also be defined as cacheable, meaning responses to them may be stored for reuse. This RFC defines GET, HEAD and POST as cacheable, although nearly all cache implementations support only GET and HEAD.
sections.plainLanguage: Three labels describe what a method promises. Safe means the server should not change anything. Idempotent means doing it twice is the same as doing it once. Cacheable means the answer may be kept. A crawler that only uses safe methods can follow every link it finds without risk.

sections.title: Content Negotiation
sections.content:
When a response carries information, the origin server often has different ways of representing it, in different formats, languages or encodings. Different users and user agents also have different capabilities and preferences. HTTP provides mechanisms for the two sides to agree.

In proactive negotiation, the user agent states its preferences in the request and the server picks, comparing what is available against the explicit negotiation fields and against implicit characteristics such as the client's network address. A Vary header field is often sent to say which parts of the request were used. The RFC lists the disadvantages: the server cannot know what is best for a given user, describing capabilities in every request wastes bandwidth and leaks information, it complicates the server, and it limits how well responses can be shared through caches. A client also cannot rely on its preferences being honoured, since the server may decide that sending something else is better than sending a 406.

In reactive negotiation, the server sends a list of the alternative representations and the user agent chooses, either automatically or through a menu, by making a further request for the one it wants. This is useful when the response varies over common dimensions such as type, language or encoding, and when shared caches carry the load. Its cost is the size of the list and the extra round trip. The 300 and 406 responses carry the list of alternatives in this form.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways to agree on which form to send. The client can say up front what it accepts and let the server choose, or the server can send a list of what it has and let the client pick. The first saves a round trip; the second suits shared caches.

sections.title: Response Status Codes
sections.content:
The status code is a three-digit integer giving the result of the attempt to understand and satisfy the request. Status codes are extensible, and a client is not required to understand every registered code, but it must understand the class, which the first digit gives, and must treat an unrecognised code as the x00 code of that class. A client must not cache a response with an unrecognised status code.

The five classes are 1xx for informational, meaning the request was received and processing continues; 2xx for successful, meaning the request was received, understood and accepted; 3xx for redirection, meaning further action is needed to complete the request; 4xx for a client error, meaning the request has bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled; and 5xx for a server error, meaning the server failed to fulfil an apparently valid request.

The reason phrases are only recommendations and can be replaced with local equivalents. Among the redirection codes, 301 says the resource has a new permanent URI, 302 says it resides temporarily under a different URI, 303 says the user agent should perform a retrieval request against a different URI and treat the result as the answer to the original request, and 307 says the resource resides temporarily under a different URI and the method must not change on redirection. For historical reasons a user agent may change the method from POST to GET after a 301 or a 302, and the RFC points at 307 for when that is not wanted.
sections.plainLanguage: The first digit of a status code says what kind of outcome it was: the request was still being processed, it worked, it needs a redirect, the request was at fault, or the server was at fault. The exact numbers are refinements of that, and the wording after them is only a suggestion.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says most security concerns about HTTP semantics are about securing the server-side application behind the HTTP interface, securing the user agent's handling of payloads, or secure use of the Internet in general, rather than about the security of the protocol itself.

It then lists the attacks that follow from the semantics this document defines. Origin servers often map the request URI onto the local file system, and most file systems are not designed to withstand malicious names. A path component that means the parent directory, or a name that reaches a system device, can turn a request into a denial of service or a disclosure of files that were never meant to be served.

Data in a request cannot be trusted. A method, a target, a header field or a body can be built so that its contents are read as a command, as code or as a query when the server passes them through a command invocation, a language interpreter or a database interface. The SQL injection attack is the familiar example. The RFC's advice is that request data should not be used in contexts that process it as instructions: parameters should be compared against fixed strings and acted on as a result of that comparison, rather than passed through an interface that is not prepared for untrusted input. The same care is needed when request data is stored and later processed, such as in log files or monitoring tools.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol itself is not the weak point; the server behind it is. The RFC warns about turning a request path into a file path by accident, and about passing request data straight into a command, a script or a database query, where it might be read as instructions.
